text: You're given a list of meeting times. Each room can hold one meeting at a time. What's the minimum number of rooms you need?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — if one meeting ends at five and another starts at five, can they share a room? And is the list ever empty?
Yes, they can share a room. And there's always at least one meeting.
Okay. One thing I want to say early: the minimum number of rooms is the largest number of meetings happening at the same moment. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth meetings, with times between zero and ten to the sixth.

Got it. Let me check the examples. Zero to thirty, five to ten, fifteen to twenty: zero to thirty overlaps each of the others, but those two don't overlap each other, so two rooms. Seven to ten and two to four never overlap, so one room. Both match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would count, at every meeting's start time, how many meetings are running, which is quadratic. This problem reminds me of a sweep line with a min-heap. I walk through time in order of start, and the heap holds the end time of every room in use. The smallest end tells me the earliest room to free up.
Does the sort order matter? Could you sort by end time instead?

It matters a lot. Popping a room means it's already free right now, so now has to move forward, which means processing meetings by start time. If I sort by end, time can jump backward. With zero to three, one to four, two to seven, and five to six, the meeting five to six comes before two to seven, pops the first two rooms, and I end up with two instead of three. Both official examples still pass with that bug, but I checked about eight hundred thousand small cases and over a hundred thousand fail.

Here's the plan, in three steps. Sort by start. For each meeting, first pop every room whose end is at or before this start. Then push this meeting's end, and record the heap size as a candidate answer. One thing worth flagging — the pop condition is less than or equal, because back-to-back meetings can share a room.

Alright. Sort by start, a min-heap of ints, and a room counter. In the loop I pop while the top is at most the current start, push the current end, and take the max of the heap size and room. One small but real detail: the heap's size is an unsigned size type, and room is an int. Standard max needs both arguments to be the same type, so without a cast to int, it doesn't even compile. The cast is safe here, since the heap never holds more than ten to the fourth items.

Let's dry-run zero to three, one to four, two to seven, five to six. Expected three. The moment that matters is two to seven: it's time two, nothing has ended yet, so the heap holds three, four, and seven, and the size hits three. At five to six, I pop three and four, which really have ended by then. Corner cases: one meeting needs one room. All identical meetings need n rooms. A back-to-back chain needs just one.

Let me think about complexity here. Sorting is n log n. Each meeting is pushed once and popped at most once, each in log n, so time is n log n overall. Space is linear for the heap, in the worst case when every meeting overlaps.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned the question into the maximum overlap at any moment. You explained why the sort must be by start, with a concrete case where sorting by end breaks. And you knew why the size needs a cast before going into max. Good work.
